The accurate bandgap prediction of perovskites has great significance for solar cell devices. Although density 
functional theory can be used for the calculations of material bandgaps, this method requires rich material 
calculation knowledge, and there are often some questions about whether the results are consistent with actual

ABX3-type perovskites on the bandgaps by using the SHAP value, and they can be well explained in physics.

of perovskite for solar cell devices.

performance potential, simple fabrication process [1–4], and low ma
terial cost. Through the development in recent years, power conversion

bandgap prediction model (BPM) of ABX3-type perovskites. Advantages: 
i) fast, it is particularly suitable for the screening of a super variety of 
different combinations, for instance, ABX3-type perovskites, and ii) ML 
can maintain excellent prediction accuracy. 
In material experiments, the traditional trial and error method not 
only consumes a lot of resources, but also wastes a lot of time. ML be
longs to the branch of artificial intelligence, which is to imitate human 
learning behavior, improve its own performance through continuous 
learning of data, and finally make predictions on unknown data [16]. 
The ML process generally includes: database establishment and clean
ing, feature variable extraction and screening, algorithm selection and 
tuning, model evaluation and interpretation. ML has huge application 
prospects in the field of materials. For example: assistance with density 
functional theory (DFT) calculation; design and optimize structure of 
PSC; analysis of the formation mechanism of materials; reduction 
experimental testing time, etc [17–21]. 
Up to now, many scholars have brought ML method into the field of 
computational materials. Yıldırım et al. built a database containing 404 
PSC stability data, using the apriori algorithm in ML to analyze the in
fluence of PSC materials, manufacturing processes, and storage condi
tions on cell stability [22]. Lu et al. used the ML algorithm to assist DFT 
calculations and found six orthorhombic lead-free HOIPs with suitable 
bandgap for solar cells and room temperature thermal stability from 
5158 undiscovered hybrid organic-inorganic perovskites (HOIPs) [23]. 
Weng et al. guided the design of new oxide perovskite catalysts and 
improved the activity of oxygen evolution reaction (OER) by the Sym
bolic regression (SR) algorithm in ML [24]. G.Pilania predicted the 
bandgaps of the double perovskites by using the KRR algorithm and the 
DFT method and the RMSE was around 0.37eV [25]. Zheng used the 
bandgap data of 102 ABX3-type perovskites in the Materials Projects 
library and random forest (RF) algorithm to establish a BPM with an 
RMSE of 0.0858 eV [26]. 
In our work, the use of the experimental data derived from experi
mental reports (227 data points of experimental values collected from 
1254 published papers) ensures that our BPMs is more realistic. By 
testing 24 kinds of BPMs generated by 4 kinds of databases and 6 kinds 
of algorithms, the data relevance and the accuracy of the models are 
guaranteed. Through the means of ML explanation (SHapley Additive 
exPlanations, abbreviated as SHAP), it is found that the contents of B- 
site metal and X-site halogen ion have the key influence on the bandgaps 
of ABX3-type perovskites. Finally, the results are explained from the 
physics. Compared with the existing reports using ML to predict 
bandgaps of PSCs, this work has the following advantages: i) The data 
used in this work are all from the experimental values in published 
related papers; ii) In the field of PSC, our work uses the Xtreme Gradient 
Boosting (Xgboost) algorithm, and the accuracy of BPM based on this 
algorithm is also second to none in the relevant literature; iii) Explaining 
the prediction patterns of ML models may be more important than the 
prediction performance of ML models, so we propose an interpretable 
ML strategy and prove its correctness. The present work uses the SHAP 
to explain the ML model and evaluates the main chemical compositions 
affecting the bandgaps of ABX3-type perovskites for the first time. 
Finally, not only can the physical laws that cause the bandgaps of ABX3- 
type perovskites change be explored from the perspective of ML, but the 
calculated results are faster and more accurate than DFT.

“power source”, and the processing and cleaning of the chemical data is 
equivalent to the “wire”, so that the power is transmitted to the “bulb” 
(machine learning) through the wire. ML algorithms are like “filaments” 
to ensure that the light bulb emits light and illuminate bandgaps of 
ABX3-type perovskites. 
The first step is to search articles by using the keyword “perovskite 
bandgap” in the web of science according to relevance, and then 
download them in ACS, nature, science, wiley, Elsevier and other. In the 
process of data collection, we find that the ABX3-type perovskites have 
the largest data and are widely used. Therefore, regardless of the quality 
of the data or the frequency of the data, the ABX3-type perovskites are 
the first choice for the database of BPM. The A-position monovalent 
cations are usually cesium (CS+), methylammonium(MA+/CH3NH3
+), 
formamidinium(FA+/NH2CHNH2
+); the B-position divalent metal ions 
are usually lead(Pb2+), Tin(Sn2+); the C-position halogen anions are 
iodide (I−), bromide (Br−), chloride (Cl−). For ABX3-type perovskites, 
the bandgaps are mainly determined by the chemical composition due to 
the fixed structure. Therefore, we choose the above 8 chemical com

ABX3-type perovskites.

“Examinee” settings: We use six ML algorithms by Scikit-learn and 
Xgboost modules to build BPMs on the pycharm platform. Linear 
regression (LR): LR is a model that uses the best linear relationship be
tween input and output to fit. K-nearest neighbors (KNN): KNN is simply 
summarized as “those who are close to you are red, those who are close 
to you are black”, i.e. your category is inferred from your neighbors. 
Support vector regression (SVR): SVR uses a linear function in vector 
space to fit the samples. The model takes the combined distance of all the 
samples’ actual positions to this linear function as the loss and mini
mizes the loss to get the parameters of the linear function. Random forest 
(RF): Random forest is representative of ensemble learning ideas. By 
integrating many decision trees into a forest, they learn from each 
other’s strengths, and finally optimize the prediction model. Multilayer 
Perceptron (MLP), which is the most commonly used type of neural 
network, consists of an input layer, an output layer, and one or more 
hidden layers. Xtreme Gradient Boosting (Xgboost): Xgboost is a branch 
of ensemble learning different from RF, which is an improvement of the 
Gradient Boosting decision tree algorithm. 
For the above models, we optimize the models by adding “Grid
SearchCV” and “10-fold cross-validation”, in order to find the hyper
parameters that make the model optimize the best performance. 
“Teacher” setting: The responsibility of the “teacher” is to evaluate the 
performance of the “candidate” (algorithm model) and select the best 
model.Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) is the most commonly used 
evaluation indicator for ML model which measures the deviation be
tween the observed value and the predicted value. In this statistics, 
Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) is often used to represent the cor
relation between two variables, which we use to test the performance of 
ML models. 0.8–1.0 is very strong correlation; 0.6–0.8 is strong corre
lation; 0.4–0.6 is moderate correlation; 0.2–0.4 is weak correlation; 
0–0.2 is no correlation or very weak correlation. 
SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP): Shapley value originated 
from cooperative game theory. Many complex ML models tend to have 
better accuracy in making predictions than ordinary linear models, but 
lack interpretability, so they are also called black box models. In 2017, 
Lundberg and Lee’s paper proposed the SHAP value as a widely appli
cable method to explain various models, making the black box model 
interpretable [27]. Before the emergence of SHAP, we often used feature 
importance or partial dependence plot to explain Xgboost and other ML 
models. Although it can directly reflect the importance of features and 
see which features have a greater impact on the final model, we cannot 
judge the relationship between features and the final prediction results. 
The SHAP value can intuitively reflect the importance of the feature 
value and the positive and negative correlation effects on the final result.

3. Results and analysis 
We set up a training dataset and a test dataset of ABX3-type perov
skites containing 204 and 23 data to train and evaluate the pros and cons 
of the algorithm. The database used is shown in Tables S1–S2 of the 
supplementary information. As shown in Fig. 2, the scattered points in 
the Taylor diagram represent the algorithm model, the radial line rep
resents the correlation coefficient (r value), the horizontal and vertical 
axes represent the standard deviation, and the dotted line represents 
RMSE. Xgboost has a degree of dispersion similar to the experimental 
value, the lowest RMSE, and the highest correlation coefficient, so 
Xgboost performs best in this set of data. This reflects the superiority of 
ensemble learning in complex data processing. The RMSE and r values of 
each algorithm are shown in Table 1. 
The establishment of ML prediction models for conduction band 
minimum (CBM) and valence band maximum(VBM). Because the data 
features are similar to features of bandgap, the prediction models of 
CBM and VBM are directly adopted the Xgboost algorithm without al
gorithm screening. The CBM and VBM databases contain 115 valid data 
points. The test set data points account for 20% of the database and are 
mutually exclusive with the training set. See Table S15 for the database. 
Fig. S2 shows the fit of our ML model, from which we can see that the 
predicted value is very close to the experimental value. Among them, the 
RMSE of the CBM prediction model is 0.11eV and the r value is 0.71, 
which shows that our ML model has a strong CBM prediction ability for 
perovskites, and the built eight features are strongly related to CBM. The 
RMSE of the VBM prediction model is 0.12eV, and the r value is 0.87, 
which shows that Xgboost’s prediction ability for VBM is also very ideal, 
and the features have a very strong correlation with VBM. The com
parison of ML predicted and experimental values of CBM and VBM are 
shown in Table S14. 
The accuracy of the BPM is mainly affected by the two factors, one is 
the applicability of the algorithm, and the other is the correlation of the 
data. For algorithms, we must adjust not only the types of algorithms, 
but also the parameters of the algorithms themselves for different data 
types. For the data itself, we not only need a huge amount of data to 
support the ML model for learning, but also to ensure the purity of the 
data itself (the same type of data with high correlation).

constitute the [BX6]4- octahedral framework [31]. The atomic level 
understanding is that the perovskite bandgap is affected by the orbital 
overlap between the metal and the halogen ions [32], which means that 
the electronic structure of the perovskite is affected by the characteris
tics of the B-X bond. Specifically, CBM and VBM are determined by the 
non-bonding hybrid state of the B-p and X-p orbitals and the 
anti-bonding hybrid states of the B-s and X-p orbitals in the B-X chain 
[33,34], so the B-X bond length and B-X-B bond angle have an important 
influence on the perovskite bandgap [35]. With the change of metal 
ions, the tilt angle between [BX6]4- octahedrons changes. When the bond 
angle of B-X-B decreases, the bandgap of ABX3-type perovskites will 
increase. For example, there are AGeI3, ASnI3 and APbI3, the B-X-B bond 
angles are 166.27◦, 159.61◦and 155.19◦, their bandgap is AGeI3
<ASnI3<APbI3 [33,36,37]. As the radius of the halogen ions decreases 
(I−(220 R/pm) > Br−(196 R/pm) > Cl−(181 R/pm)), the B-X bond 
length decreases, resulting in an increase in the force between X ions and 
B ions, which weakens the absorption capacity of the perovskite in the 
long wave region, that is to say the band gap is widened. From the 
perspective of ion electronegativity, as the electronegativity of X ions 
increases, it will also lead to an increase in the bandgap [38,39]. The 
theory of bond length and bond angle explains why B-metal ions and 
X-halogen ions have a great influence on the change of the perovskite 
bandgap, which also proves the correctness of the judgment we obtained 
through the SHAP explanation. 
Through SHAP’s explanation of the ML model, we know the main 
influence of the B-site metal and X-site halogen ion on the bandgap of 
ABX3-type perovskites, and then use the published papers to explore the 
physical explanation of the effect of the B-X bond length and B-X-B bond 
angle on the bandgap. Finally, we continue to verify the influence of the 
B-site metal and X-site halogen ion on the B-X bond length and B-X-B 
bond angle, and further explain the effect of B-site metal and X-site 
halogen ion on the bandgap control. The atomic-level explanation of the 
adjustment of the B-site metal and X-site halogen ion on the bandgap is 
the effect of bond length and bond angle on the electronic properties of 
ABX3-type perovskites. As shown in Fig. 7 (a), the change of bond length 
is calculated by the DFT. Due to the reduction of metal ion radius, the 
average bond length (3.19 Å) of Pb–I is slightly larger than that of Sn–I 
(3.16 Å). We further calculate the change of bond angle. As shown in 
Fig. 7(b), the crystal structure of MASnxPb1-xI3 will undergo a phase 
change when near x = 0.5, from I4cm space group (Pb-rich composi
tions) to P4mm space group (Sn-rich compositions). The change of the 
space group is caused by the rotation of the [BX6]4- octahedron in the 
opposite direction (out-of-phase tilting) perpendicular to the crystallo
graphic c-axis, resulting in a change in the B-X-B bond angle [40]. We 
calculated that the tilting angle of MAPbI3 is 167.63◦(163.55◦[40]), 
and the calculated inclination angle is 174◦~175◦when x > 0.5, which 
is slightly smaller than the experimental data 177.4◦for MASnI3 [40]. 
The increase of the Sn doping ratio leads to the increase of the B-X-B 
bond angle, which is reflected in the bandgap reduction and consistent 
with the references (The change of bandgap for MASnxPb1-xI3 is shown 
in Table 2). As shown in Table 3, since the ion radius of Br−is less than 
I−, the bond length of B-X decreases with the increase of Br doping ratio, 
which is reflected in the increase of bandgap. We have proved that the 
ratio of metal and halogen ions controls the bandgap by the DFT 
calculation and relevant references. 
As shown in Tables 2 and 3, for the bandgap calculation of 
MASnxPb1-xI3, the RMSE between the predicted ML value and the 
experimental value is 0.049 eV; the RMSE between the calculated DFT 
value and the experimental value is 0.052 eV. For the bandgap calcu
lation of CsPb(BrxI1-x)3, the RMSE of the predicted ML value and the 
experimental value is 0.08 eV, and the RMSE of the calculated DFT value 
and the experimental value is 0.105 eV. Through comparison, it can be 
seen that our ML model can not only accurately predict the controlling 
effect of the ratio of metal and halide ions on the bandgap, but also is 
more accurate than the DFT calculated value.

graphic c-axis, resulting in a change in the B-X-B bond angle [40]. We 
calculated that the tilting angle of MAPbI3 is 167.63◦(163.55◦[40]), 
and the calculated inclination angle is 174◦~175◦when x > 0.5, which 
is slightly smaller than the experimental data 177.4◦for MASnI3 [40]. 
The increase of the Sn doping ratio leads to the increase of the B-X-B 
bond angle, which is reflected in the bandgap reduction and consistent 
with the references (The change of bandgap for MASnxPb1-xI3 is shown 
in Table 2). As shown in Table 3, since the ion radius of Br−is less than 
I−, the bond length of B-X decreases with the increase of Br doping ratio, 
which is reflected in the increase of bandgap. We have proved that the 
ratio of metal and halogen ions controls the bandgap by the DFT 
calculation and relevant references. 
As shown in Tables 2 and 3, for the bandgap calculation of 
MASnxPb1-xI3, the RMSE between the predicted ML value and the 
experimental value is 0.049 eV; the RMSE between the calculated DFT 
value and the experimental value is 0.052 eV. For the bandgap calcu
lation of CsPb(BrxI1-x)3, the RMSE of the predicted ML value and the 
experimental value is 0.08 eV, and the RMSE of the calculated DFT value 
and the experimental value is 0.105 eV. Through comparison, it can be 
seen that our ML model can not only accurately predict the controlling 
effect of the ratio of metal and halide ions on the bandgap, but also is 
more accurate than the DFT calculated value.
